Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

In a letter sent to SEC Chair Atkins, Sens. Warren and Van Hollen said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws.

Top Democrats Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen are demanding that Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins take down its crypto rulemaking governing how crypto projects can raise capital and how tokenized securities can be traded.

In two separate letters sent to Atkins on Tuesday, Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Tina Smith and other Senate Banking Committee members said the agency's "Regulation Crypto Assets" would allow crypto firms to circumvent securities laws, weaken state jurisdiction and could harm investors.

"The proposal would create a new 'tailored securities offering regime' for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets," the senators wrote. "However, the proposal only serves to help crypto assets escape from the SEC's regulatory regime and gives them special treatment—with less oversight—compared to other traditional securities."

In August, the SEC proposed crypto offering rules to offer startup and fundraising exemptions for digital asset offerings. It allows for a "startup exemption" that would exempt offerings of up to $5 million from registration rules under the Securities Act of 1933 for four years — a federal law focused on anti-fraud and requiring certain disclosures. The proposal also includes a "fundraising exemption" for offerings up to $75 million for a year.

Warren is poised to take on a more prominent role following Democrats’ victories in November's midterm elections, which handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Warren has been critical of crypto in the past and has particularly brought up concerns around illicit finance and money laundering. Meanwhile, Van Hollen could be the next Senate Majority Leader. He has since challenged current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for that role.

Sens. Jack Reed and Tina Smith join the two in the second letter asking the SEC to withdraw its innovation exemption — a measure released in September to bring capital markets onchain through the trading of tokenized stocks. It is a five-year exemption that would exempt certain trading venues, called tokenized securities venues, from being defined as an exchange and also exempts specific liquidity providers from being defined as a dealer under securities law when they trade stocks or provide liquidity through automated market makers.

The senators said it would allow platforms to operate outside of certain safeguards, including involving fair pricing and market transparency.

"The order would allow TSV platforms to operate a shadow stock market outside longstanding regulatory protections designed to ensure fair and transparent markets, impose new burdens on publicly traded companies seeking to protect their shareholders, and create unnecessary risks of illicit financial activity," the senators wrote.

The three senators also said the innovation exemption could cause capital markets to splinter.

"As concerned stakeholders have pointed out, fragmenting our securities markets by creating a lightly regulated alternative marketplace for tokenized securities unnecessarily risks dividing liquidity into isolated pools and expanding opportunities for corrosive regulatory arbitrage," they said.

A separate group of Senate Democrats have also brought up concerns about the innovation exemption. Last week, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto said it could open the door for illicit finance actors and also had concerns about protections for retail investors around pricing.

#5013. Florida Man Jailed for Using AI to Pose as Streamer N3ON in $260K Crypto Scam

Florida Man Jailed for Using AI to Pose as Streamer N3ON in $260K Crypto Scam

A Port St. Lucie, Florida, man has been sentenced to 47 months in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate popular streamer N3ON and con a meme coin project's organizers out of roughly $260,000 in crypto.

David Anthony Sanchez, 36, who also went by "Dave the Jewler" and other aliases, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Melissa Damian after pleading guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida said on Tuesday. He was also ordered to pay restitution to his victims.

A Port St. Lucie man was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate a popular online streamer and deceive investors in a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that caused approximately $260,000 in losses. The case serves as a warning that… pic.twitter.com/4DZnaiaPNt

— US Attorney's Office Southern District of Florida (@USAO_SDFL) November 24, 2026

According to court records, Sanchez set up online accounts made to look as though they belonged to N3ON, and contacted the organizers of a crypto meme coin project while posing as both the streamer and his representative.

He signed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent the organizers an AI-generated voice recording that mimicked the streamer, falsely confirming that N3ON would endorse, promote and take part in the project, prosecutors said. Believing the deal was real, the organizers sent about $260,000 in crypto to accounts Sanchez controlled.

Sanchez then converted much of the crypto into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to hide where the money came from and who owned it, and spent it on himself, according to prosecutors. The press release did not name the meme coin project.

"The defendant exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate the trust of unsuspecting victims and deprive them of their money," Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in a statement.

The case is a small example of a fast-growing type of crypto fraud. Impersonation scams grew more than 1,400% year on year in 2025, driven in part by AI tools, as crypto scam losses reached a record $17 billion, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated in January.

AI deepfakes of government officials, billionaires and celebrities accounted for 40% of high-value crypto frauds in 2024, according to a report from crypto exchange Bitget. Earlier this month, the Justice Department said North Korean hackers had stolen more than $400 million in crypto over 18 months through a scheme it calls "FaceStealer," which uses recorded webcam footage and deepfake videos to impersonate victims' trusted contacts on video calls. The same tactics have been used to target crypto workers.

Legislation aimed at the problem has stalled. The AI Fraud Deterrence Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Neal Dunn (R-FL) in November 2025, would raise penalties for AI-assisted fraud.

AI-assisted money laundering, one of the charges Sanchez pleaded guilty to, would carry fines of up to $1 million or three times the value of the transaction, alongside up to 20 years in prison. The bill has not advanced beyond the House Judiciary Committee.

LayerZero LayerZero (ZRO) has named Kakao Pay, Samsung Card, and ZAN as new validators for Zero, its blockchain network expected to launch on Nov. 30.

The three will join the upcoming mainnet as genesis validators and help secure the network's consensus and proof-verification system at launch. Four Pillars, a South Korean blockchain research firm, will operate the validator node on behalf of Samsung Card.

Samsung Card, a subsidiary of South Korea's largest conglomerate, had approximately 13.92 million cardholders as of the end of September. ZAN is the Web3 infrastructure platform backed by Ant Digital Technologies that provides node services across more than 80 chains.

LayerZero co-founder and CEO Bryan Pellegrino said the additions of Asian financial heavyweights are meant to give Zero a more globally distributed set of validators from the start.

"The future of global markets needs Better Markets Technology: infrastructure that matches not only the speed and borderless nature of tokenized assets, but the structural resilience of globally distributed ecosystems," Pellegrino said. "We're thrilled to partner with some of Asia's most influential financial services firms to bring that vision to life with a truly global set of validators."

The Layer 1 blockchain is designed primarily for institutional and global financial markets. Unlike most blockchains that re-execute every transaction, the chain uses ZK proofs to separate execution from verification, removing a layer of redundancy by leaving validators to only verify the proofs, LayerZero said.

Zero is scheduled to go live on Nov. 30 alongside LayerZero's ATLAS trading infrastructure. Staked ZRO will be distributed equally across genesis validators until March 31, 2027.

Kakao Pay CEO Shin Won-keun said the company plans to explore the Zero network to bridge traditional finance and onchain markets, including initiatives based on stablecoins pegged to the South Korean won.

#5009. House Committee advances Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill with narrow path to passage

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

The House Financial Services Committee has advanced H.R. 8957, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, which would codify a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and impose a minimum 20-year lock on federally held bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC).

The legislation, introduced on May 21 by Rep. Nick Begich, would allow the Treasury secretary to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile for other cryptocurrencies 180 days after enactment.

Once deposited in the reserve, bitcoin cannot be "sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose" for at least 20 years. The bill also includes transparency requirements such as proof-of-reserve reporting and directs federal agencies to report existing holdings.

On Sept. 16, the House Financial Services Committee approved it on a party-line vote of 28-21, with support from every Republican representative and opposition from every Democrat. On Nov. 24, the committee officially sent the revised bill to the full House, where it is now eligible for a floor vote.

The bill builds on U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order issued in March 2025 that directed the creation of a bitcoin reserve funded mainly through bitcoin already owned by the government from criminal or civil forfeitures, and a separate digital asset stockpile. The order sparked concern from some lawmakers on bitcoin's riskiness and volatility.

While the bill is now on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789, its chances of passing are low. The current 119th Congress is expected to adjourn in the coming weeks, leaving little time for a House floor vote, Senate consideration, and final passage before the session ends.

Polymarket odds show a 4% chance of the U.S. establishing a national bitcoin reserve by the end of this year, down from 60% around a year ago and 34% in May this year.

If the bill fails to pass within this Congress, it would have to be reintroduced in the 120th Congress. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve created by the March 2025 executive order would remain in place, but a future president could alter or reverse it without congressional approval. Reintroducing and advancing the initiative may face steeper challenges as Democrats are set to control both chambers starting in January.

#5008. French Senate Rejects Plan to Make Crypto Holders Declare Self-Custody Wallets

French Senate Rejects Plan to Make Crypto Holders Declare Self-Custody Wallets

France's Senate has rejected a proposal that would have required crypto holders to declare self-custodied wallets worth more than €100,000 ($110,000) to tax authorities, according to the official record of Tuesday's debate on the 2027 budget.

Two identical amendments, one from the Communist-led CRCE-K group and one from a group of senators led by Anne-Sophie Romagny, were voted down after both the government and the Senate's finance committee opposed them. The vote was earlier reported by Cointelegraph.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The amendments would have obliged holders to declare self-custodied crypto above the threshold. French taxpayers already have to declare crypto accounts held on platforms, but not crypto held in their own wallets.

"The shop window is illuminated, but the back room remains in the dark," CRCE-K senator Alexandre Basquin said, in comments translated from French. The more closely platforms are monitored, the greater the incentive for large holders to keep their crypto themselves, he argued.

Minister for Public Action and Accounts David Amiel said the EU's DAC8 directive, which requires crypto service providers to report users' transactions to tax authorities, had already brought transparency. A purely declarative obligation would not let authorities track how crypto is used in money laundering or tax fraud cases, he said.

The proposal had already passed through France's lower house. The National Assembly's finance committee backed it in October, prompting a backlash from the crypto industry.

The budget was later rejected in the lower house, so the Senate is debating the government's original bill, without the crypto amendments that deputies had added.

On Tuesday, senators also rejected an amendment that would have made swaps from crypto into stablecoins a taxable event. Amiel argued that stablecoins are not money, as they have no legal tender status and are often unstable. A proposal to extend France's exit tax to crypto holdings worth more than €800,000 ($877,000) was also defeated.

Critics of the reporting plan had warned that a register of large crypto holders could become a target in France, which has become the global epicenter of "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto.

France's national anti-organized crime prosecutor's office recorded more than 70 crypto-linked kidnappings and unlawful detentions in the first eight months of 2026, Decrypt reported in September. Authorities charged 88 people, including minors, in a crackdown in April.

Leaks of personal data have added to those fears. A breach of France's tax authority in August exposed records tied to more than 678,000 people and businesses. In January, a tax agent was accused of looking up crypto investors and prison guards in tax databases for an unidentified buyer, Le Parisien reported, while a June attack in Nancy followed a data breach at French crypto tax platform Waltio.

Galaxy now treats a daily close below $58,525, the June 30 closing low, as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy has withdrawn its October call that bitcoin's bear market ended in June, warning that the world's largest cryptocurrency could move even lower when it breaks the June level.

In a research note released Wednesday, Alex Thorn, head of firmwide research at Galaxy, wrote that the team's previous technical argument is "no longer valid" and that the team now treats a daily close below $58,525 — the June 30 closing low — as the start of a move toward a materially lower low.

Galaxy's revised outlook comes as the crypto market remained volatile. Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) rose 2.4% over the past 24 hours to trade at $60,677 as of 10:50 p.m. ET Wednesday, after falling to as low as around $57,300 earlier in the day, according to The Block's BTC price page. Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) climbed 2.1% to $1,695, BNB gained 3.2%, and XRP added 4.2%.

Last month, Thorn had suggested that bitcoin's bear market ended in June. He cited Galaxy's September reclaim of the 50-week moving average, a level that has historically served as a ceiling during bear markets. However, Thorn's latest note points out that after seven weekly closes above the average, bitcoin closed back below it in early November and later closed below the 200-week average.

"[Although] bitcoin has until about Dec. 8 to regain the average, we must acknowledge that the bear market is very likely not over and that the reclaim is unlikely to come in time," Thorn said in the note. "Previously, no reclaim of this kind had been followed by a new low."

Galaxy said that a daily close below $58,525 would be a "break of a standing low," adding that in all seven prior bear markets when bitcoin broke a similar standing low, the prices fell at least another 17%.

The firm also noted that the macro backdrop has deteriorated since June. On Nov. 19, the two-year Treasury yield was 0.88 percentage point above the fed funds rate — "a sign that the market is pricing a higher policy rate ahead," Thorn said. Also, the S&P 500 was 1.5% below its record at the June low and closed 11.6% below it on Nov. 20, according to the report.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products have shed 71,339 BTC ($4.95 billion) since Oct. 4, with outflows on 22 of 35 sessions, according to Galaxy. That left holdings at an estimated 1.24 million BTC, 9.7% below the Oct. 9, 2025, peak.

"Whether Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia on Nov. 23 can be the spark that pulls bitcoin back up to levels needed to end the bear market is unknown," Thorn added.

Thorn said traders should watch whether bitcoin can hold its June lows of $58,525 on a daily close and $59,517 on a weekly closing basis. "A weekly close back above the 200-week average, then the 50-week average, would bring us back toward our October view," Thorn said.

Beyond the technical levels, the firm is also watching whether financial advisors increase their bitcoin ETP holdings and whether the two-year Treasury yield moves back toward the fed funds rate.

#5002. Morning Minute: Ethereum Focuses on Security As AI Threats Rise

Morning Minute: Ethereum Focuses on Security As AI Threats Rise

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and made cryptography its top priority. The reason isn’t quantum computers.

Protocol lead Kev Wedderburn wrote this week that “recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk”, and the distinction matters. The quantum threat has always been a hardware problem, and hardware problems announce themselves years in advance because somebody has to build the machine. The AI version is a math problem. A sufficiently capable model could find a structural shortcut in the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin, and it would need no special hardware to do it.

Researcher Justin Drake raised the scenario in October. In a worst case, he said, existing signatures could become vulnerable within months.

An Anthropic mathematician named Levent Alpöge posted a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with an unreleased version of Claude, along with a formalized proof archive. Nobody has verified it. It doesn’t break elliptic curve cryptography and nobody is claiming it does. What it does is demonstrate the capability class Drake was describing, roughly a month after he described it.

Axios reported Tuesday that more than two dozen people familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic say employees worry their most advanced unreleased models may never be safe enough to release. The concerns named include reward hacking, models that hide or misrepresent their reasoning, and systems capable enough to find weaknesses in the safety measures their own developers built. OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed Sunday that labs agree on shared limits on how far they train models.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The plan replaces elliptic curves with hash-based cryptography, which rests on fewer structural assumptions about mathematics. It touches how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how layer-2 data gets verified. Drake proposed pulling the deadline from December 2029 to December 2028. Ethlabs withdrew its faster-block-production proposal from the Hegotá upgrade to free up engineers. The Foundation has deployed AI agents to hunt bugs in its own infrastructure, which is a reasonable response and also an admission about where the advantage currently sits.

Wedderburn’s own framing: it’s harder than the Merge, and there’s less time. He also acknowledged that moving faster makes it easier to ship bugs.

Bitcoin is on the same road. Blockstream’s Jonas Nick published a security analysis of SHRINCS last week, the apparent frontrunner to replace Bitcoin’s signatures, with sizes running from 548 bytes to 5,777 against today’s 64 to 71.

So the AI threat is looming (and accelerating), but the two largest crypto assets have teams that are responding. Now we wait on action, and more assurances that crypto is safe from AI threats. Assurances that could ensure the bottom is in fact in, if and when they arrive…

Zcash developers urged users to move funds out of an older shielded transaction pool over concerns that AI advances could compromise its cryptography.

Zcash development team Zakura urged the community to accelerate the proposed retirement of Sapling, an older shielded transaction pool, which holds nearly 2% of the total Zcash token supply.

Zakura, led by co-founder Sean Bowe and developer Dev Ojha, told community members on Wednesday to start migrating their funds from Sapling, which holds about 400,000 Zcash (ZEC) tokens, worth about $302 million.

Zakura recommended a network upgrade to stop new deposits into Sapling, while keeping withdrawals open to allow existing holders to migrate their funds to Zcash’s newer shielded pool, Ironwood.

AI-accelerated mathematical advancements could eventually undermine Sapling’s pairing-based cryptography and put funds at risk by allowing attackers to forge transaction proofs and potentially create counterfeit ZEC, Zakura warned. Ironwood uses a different proof system that does not rely on similar pairings. Dev Ojha proposed making the Sapling pool withdrawal-only in April 2026.

On June 3, Zcash developers temporarily suspended Orchard transactions after discovering a vulnerability in the shielded pool. Functionality was restored later that day through an emergency upgrade. The Zcash Foundation said there was no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited.

#4996. The 12 Best Swim Trunks for Men of 2026, Worn and Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our editors recommend shorts from Rhone and Fair Harbor.

SUMMER MAY BE behind us, but that doesn’t mean your swim trunks need to go into hibernation. If you’re planning to escape the cold for somewhere sunny this winter, a good pair should be in your suitcase. The beauty of men’s swim trunks is that they can be worn in or out of the water, doubling as the ultimate beachside bottoms or everyday shorts. The best swim trunks for men today have a moisture-wicking and quick-drying fabric, four-way stretch for mobility, a flattering length, and an athletic fit. Finding the right one for you can be a challenge, which is why we're here to help. Our team of fashion editors spent the past year trying and testing swim trunks to find options that blend comfort and style.

Over the past four years, I’ve tested more than 20 different pairs of swim trunks—everything from legacy surf brands to buzzy newcomers—but Fair Harbor’s have consistently exceeded my expectations. This pair nails that trifecta of being stylish, functional, and worth the price.

The first thing I noticed: the fabric. It’s a cotton-poly blend that feels smooth and broken-in right out of the gate. It doesn’t feel like any of that stiff, swishy, overly synthetic feel you get with most swim trunks. I’m usually quick to write off built-in liners altogether, but the BreezeKnit liner changed my mind. It feels more like a supportive pair of boxer briefs than the usual scratchy mesh. It’s snug (but comfortable on the crown jewels), breathable, and, most importantly, it doesn’t ride up or chafe. I’ve worn it for full beach days in Puerto Rico—swimming, walking, grabbing lunch—and never once felt the need to adjust.

The 7-inch inseam hits just above the knee on me, giving it a clean, tailored look. It’s an easy middle ground that works whether you’re getting in the water or just wearing it as your default summer short. There’s enough stretch in the cotton-polyester fabric that I never feel restricted. Plus, it comes in seersucker versions, solid-colored options, and other unique patterns. The hidden zipper pocket stashes a key or card without them slipping out, and the side pockets don’t balloon up in the water—something a lot of trunks still get wrong. It’s not a substitute for a gym short, but the fabric dries quickly for other oceanside activities.

I can’t get enough of the R&R Trunk's timeless style, functional fabric, and flattering fit. I love the no-fuss design with a tailored cut that’s not too baggy or slim. Coupled with the flexible waistband, the fit looks great on most body types. It’s available in two inseams–5.5 and 7.5 inches. The latter provides enough coverage and hits a couple inches above the knee for most men (our universal style recommendation for shorts). Though I wore the shorter length on the beach during my stay in Miami because it shows off my summer leg gains.

Rhone’s athleisure performs just as well as it looks. I’ve sweat-tested the R&R during beachside runs and volleyball games, and found that its odor-fighting fabric kept me feeling fresh. The mesh liner kept my family jewels locked in, without cutting off circulation. A few editors on our style team who have the R&R trunk say that the liner really does have a second-skin like quality. That’s probably because the polyester blend fabric is stretchy, which felt more comfortable than Lululemon’s (also great!) Swim Short. These durable features also mean the R&R Trunk doubles as a decent gym short if you’re in a pinch, and saves you one less thing to pack for a tropical vacation. We love that it comes in 11 colorways, but if you want to go classic, you can’t go wrong with the Electric Blue or Navy option.

The absence of liner offers a comfortable commando style, which is why I prefer a pair like this one from Lululemon. I don’t have to be bothered with any mesh material that feels restrictive or scratchy against my crown jewels—I can just slip it on and head into the water. I also love that the minimal design doesn’t scream “swim trunk”, so I can go from brunch to the boardwalk or the pool without having to do an outfit change. It passes as an everyday short, which is exactly the kind of versatility I want in the summer. The polyester-elastomultiester fabric has so much stretch, it performs just as good—if not better—than most of my gym shorts.

I’ve worn this pair for pickup volleyball and quick workouts, and they move with you instead of clinging or sagging out. It also dries fast and doesn't get that heavy, waterlogged feel after a swim, which makes a huge difference if you’re posted up poolside for a while. The 7-inch inseam is short enough to show some quad, but long enough that it still feels put-together if you’re grabbing a drink after. On my 5’8” frame, it lands a couple inches above the knee with a clean, tailored look—not too baggy, not too slim. If you’re taller, it’ll read a bit shorter and sportier; shorter guys get that ideal mid-thigh cut without going full retro.

After testing Proof’s Performance Swim Trunk, we found that it’s easily the most durable short on this list. Our editors appreciate the polyester-spandex blend fabric, which is stretchy, quick drying, and nearly tear proof. We’ve sported this during tropical hikes and extreme water sports, and found that the Performance Trunk held up to just about anything mother nature threw at it. We like the moisture-wicking liner, which is actually more comfortable than Rhone’s R&R short, but we did find it didn’t dry as quickly as Rhone’s short, and is a bit thicker than we’d prefer. Still, those are minor quibbles for a swim trunk as functional as this one.

Looks-wise, the Performance Trunk isn’t the most stylish of the bunch, and it’s not meant to be. It’s available in six solid colors and two inseam options, all of which have a no-frills design. Though we have to say, because of its barebones aesthetics, the Performance Trunk looks a lot cleaner than your typical bulky hiking short. Proof markets this as a multipurpose trunk that doubles as a gym short, and after putting it through the paces, we agree with that claim. While it’s not as breathable as Ten Thousand’s award-winning Interval Short, Proof’s stretchy fabric moves easily through all sorts of workouts.

For your next vacation, you need a dressy swim trunk that can look great at the beach, bar, or restaurant. Enter this one from Bather, which has a plaid-like pattern with complementing tones of maroon and blue. This makes it more polished than your typical swim shorts, so you can easily pair it with a simple polo or the brand’s matching camp shirt and sandals for a foolproof, lunchtime fit in your arsenal. I’ve worn it to a five-star hotel’s restaurant and then straight to the pool for a mid-day cocktail.

The waistband rests gently on the waist, but you can adjust the fit using the drawstrings. Unlike the scratchy net-like liners in cheaper swim trunks, the nylon-spandex blend is silky and irritation-free, so I could wear it for hours and be comfortable. Plus, the 5.5-inch inseam flatters tall and short guys alike. In terms of functionality, the pockets are super deep for your sunglasses or wallet, while one in the back snaps shut for extra security.

Fair Harbor offers so many great trunks, we couldn't help but to feature the Anchor Short, too. It's available in a variety of solids and prints, but we're big fans of the red stripe option, since it has a cool ‘80s vibe that pairs well with laidback T-shirts, tank tops, and more. This style also comes with the BreezeKnit liner—Fair Harbor's soft, supportive alternative to traditional mesh liner found in swimwear. It provides a snug and comfortable feel, while keeping you cool as ice.

Unlike other picks on this list, The Anchor Trunk is available in three inseams. The 6-inch inseam is great for guys who want to show off their hard-earned leg gains this summer. The 8-inch inseam hits the sweet spot between casual and polished, a safe bet if you're unsure which to go for. And the 10-inch inseam is the longest option, ideal for those who prefer a bit more coverage. Plus, its relaxed (not baggy) fit keeps this from veering into Reno 911! territory.

Ralph Lauren’s classic style is the most versatile of the bunch—it works as a swim trunk, a casual short, and even a workout short. I’ve worn it for early runs along the boardwalk, knocked out quick leg circuits on vacation, and then jumped straight into the water without needing to change. The 5.75-inch inseam gives it a shorter, more athletic cut that feels mobile and unrestrictive, especially when you’re moving. But its trimmer, more style-forward look makes it clean enough to pass as an everyday short.

It’s made from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries quickly and has just enough stretch that you can bend down or twist at any turn. The mesh liner feels breathable and supportive, unlike traditional swim trunks. And because the silhouette is sleek and the design is minimal—save for that signature embroidered pony—it pairs easily with a tee or button-down, making it a true wear-all-day option for beach trips, resort hangs, or any summer day that doesn’t stick to one lane.

Sure, this is the most expensive option on our list, but we think Orlebar Brown's Bulldog Trunk packs serious style that’s worthy of its higher price point. The polyester-elastane fabric is designed with a textured stripe pattern, which is very sharp and unexpected—something most guys would shy away from, so you’ll probably be the only guy at the pool rocking it. I wore mine to the beach in Costa Rica, and no one had anything remotely close to this pair; only baggy boardshort-like types.

This one lands mid-thigh at a 6-inch inseam, which is the golden length for most men. It’s not as stretchy as the Rhone pair, but you’re not rocking this for comfort; the Bulldog is all about quiet luxury. When I’m not in the water, I wear it with just about any solid polo or camp shirt for a five-star resort fit. Plus, the gold fasteners on the waist add extra style points, and just look super plush.

If you’re looking for something more surf-specific, the California-based brand best known for its laid-back, surfer aesthetic delivers the Cruise Boardshort. It’s cut from a lightweight polyester-elastane blend that dries impressively fast, making it ideal for long days in and out of the water. The scalloped leg—where the hem curves slightly upward at the outer thigh—gives you a greater range of motion and a subtle retro-sport look. It’s one of those design tweaks that looks cool but also improves mobility.

It’s built to stay put. The double drawcord waistband adds extra security, so even when you’re getting knocked around by waves or caught in a strong current, you’re not worrying about your trunks slipping. It’s a small but clutch feature if you’re actually swimming, surfing, or doing anything more active than lounging.

Patagonia used a creative, cloudy effect across its lengthy boardshort that looks like sun-faded tie-dye you’d find on a well-traveled surf trip. It’s stylish enough to stand out amongst a sea of guys in basic trunks. Like Vuori’s option, this pair falls right above the knee, providing more coverage in case your shorts ride up as you get out of the water. I’m 5'8" and the 18-inch outseam fits pretty long on me, so the fit is more flattering for taller guys around 6’ feet. If you want things even longer, the brand also offers a 21-inch version that hovers over the knee.

Despite the trimmer leg, the cut never feels restrictive—it’s got enough room to move without baggy. It’s made with a lightweight polyester-spandex fabric that has a slightly sturdier structure than most of the swim trunks, but flexes whether you’re paddling out or diving a volleyball. I found it dries down quickly between dips, and the double looped waistband ensures it stays secure.

Patagonia’s Baggies Short has proven its durability on everything from multi-day hikes to back-to-back swimming sessions. Our guys have worn this trunk for backpacking through rugged trails, jumping into rivers, and air-drying in the sun—day after day—without wearing them out. The tough nylon fabric resists abrasion from rocks, sand, and saltwater, while the water-repellent coating helps it dry quickly.

Unlike traditional slanted pockets that can balloon up in the water, this pair has mesh openings inside, so the water flows out and doesn’t weigh you down. Despite dozens of uses and hours in the ocean, we haven’t seen these trunks fade, fray, or lose shape. Our fashion editors found they pair nicely with a string of T-shirts and sneakers for coffee pick-ups or quick grocery runs.

Sometimes, swim trunks with loud designs can be too in-your-face, but Mack Weldon went easy on this pair. It’s decked out with a dotted gradient pattern that adds a visual pop, without looking tacky. Our editors have worn this with a white polo to balance things out, and works as a foolproof fit for beachside lunches. We especially like the fit: it’s relaxed, but slimmer than the Bather swim trunks for a dressier vibe.

Like most of the swim trunks on this list, this version is made with a polyester-spandex flex that offers a lot of mobility. We could maintain a full range of motion through running, squatting and walking. During our testing, the mesh liner didn’t irritate our family jewels either. In fact, it was one of the more comfortable liners on the list.

If you're performing heavy activities in swimsuits, consider doing without liners. Board shorts, for instance, aren't made with liners for more wiggle room and comfort. Otherwise, liners should fit snugly, but should never be too tight or pinch your skin. Built-in mesh liners provide extra support to your down-there and keep everything in place as you move. Since they're mesh, they're also breathable and quick-drying.

Shorts are getting shorter, and so are swim trunks. But you don't have to chase trends. Typically, around 7 inches in inseam length is a universally flattering fit that hits a couple inches above the thigh. Though if you want to show off your quads, you can't go wrong with a 5-inch inseam, either. If you're looking at outseam lengths, 14-inch is more fashion-forward, 17-inch is a casual mid-length, and 20-inch is as full coverage as you can get without wearing pants.

If you're swimming, surfing, or just moving around a lot in bathing suits, Stafford advises stretch as a must-have factor, since it allows a great fit and range of motion in and out of the water.

Waistbands should fit comfortably on your body, and a drawstring may help you to adjust the waist size if needed. We recommend a full-elastic waistband with a drawcord because it ensures you keep your trunks on, even if you’re diving from the high dive. If you’re going for a snap closure, just make sure it’s not too tight with the ability to unsnap after one beer.

To find the best swim trunks for men, our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, spent the past five years testing more than 100 swim trunks in a variety of settings. For instance, we went whitewater rafting in Proof's performance shorts, swam laps in Rhone's R&R short, and sported Orlebar Brown swim trunks at the beach. From there, we evaluated these swim trunks based on their style, fit, price point, performance in and out of the water, and versatility to make the final top picks.

Bonus points if they doubled as athletic shorts or hiking shorts. Specifically, we looked for styles that are not trendy or trend-chasing; instead, our picks of the best swim trunks have a flattering fit, provide a ton of value at reasonable price points, and come in styles that will look great years from now.

The 12 best swim trunks for men tested by our style editors below are all quick-drying, comfortable, and look great. Whether you're planning to wear these to the beach, poolside, or to your weekend lunch, the best swim trunks for men have you covered.

Obviously, cotton is a no-go—it gets way too heavy when met with water. Our fashion team recommends lightweight synthetic fabrics since they dry quickly and are usually fade-resistant to the sun and chlorine. These synthetic fabrics are ideal for underwater wear because they won't get hefty and pull you down when drenched in water.

Poly with the addition of stretch (Lycra, elastane) material is the most common with good reason—more comfortable, forgiving. Some brands use nylon instead of poly because it absorbs less water and does not get heavy as the waterproofing wears off over time, but nylon does not (take color) dye as deeply and vibrantly as poly.

Choosing the right color and print for men's swim trunks boils down to personal style, skin tone, body type, and occasion. If you prefer a more classic and versatile look, solid colors like navy, blue, or olive are excellent choices that can easily transition from the beach to casual outings. If you want something a bit more eye-catching, subtle patterns like stripes or small geometric prints add personality without being too loud. For those who like to stand out, bright colors, tropical florals, or retro-inspired prints make a strong statement, especially on an island.

Your skin tone can also guide your choice—fairer skin tones tend to work best with earth tones and pastels, while medium to tan skin pairs well with rich blues, corals, or reds. Darker tones can pull off almost any color, but bright neons and strong contrasts pop especially well. Body type plays a factor too—shorter guys might benefit from vertical stripes or a shorter inseam to create a lengthening effect, while taller guys can balance their frame with medium-to-long inseams and bold patterns. Athletic builds look great in solid colors and tailored fits that highlight their shape, whereas stockier builds might find that darker shades or micro-prints create a more streamlined look.

Lastly, think about where you'll be wearing swim trunks. For pool parties and resort vacations, playful prints and vibrant hues add to the fun, while sporty designs with color-blocking work well for active beach days. If you're looking for swim trunks that can double as everyday shorts, muted tones or subtle patterns offer the most versatility. Ultimately, the best choice is whatever makes you feel confident and comfortable.

#4995. Bitcoin price eyes $61K as Talos warns of thin Thanksgiving liquidity

Bitcoin joined US stock futures in a modest relief rally as Talos questioned crypto demand and the broader outlook for the AI trade.

Bitcoin (BTC) reclaimed $60,000 at Wednesday’s daily close as selling pressure eased across crypto markets.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD 0.8% higher at noon UTC on Thursday, approaching $61,000.

BTC/USD 1-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US stock futures were green as the Thanksgiving holiday arrived, with both S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures trading around 0.5% higher. US markets will reopen for a shortened session on Friday.

Nasdaq 100 futures one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The recovery followed a bumpy start to the week, with markets facing uncertainty over AI spending, hot US inflation data and the prospect of new international trade tariffs.

In its latest weekly report, digital asset manager Talos questioned whether the rally following Nvidia’s decision to bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO could last. Bitcoin and stocks immediately rose on the news, which came just before Monday’s opening bell, but subsequently surrendered much of the gains.

“The rebound was not a vote of confidence in AI as a whole,” Talos wrote. Nvidia’s U-turn on Huang “removed a leadership question but did not change the macro backdrop.”

BTC price continued to track tech stocks closely. On Wednesday, Cointelegraph reported that its correlation with the Nasdaq Composite Index had reached 0.73.

Still, the equity rebound failed to draw sustained crypto buying, according to Talos, which said spot and derivatives order books still favored sellers.

“BTC’s muted rebound shows the relief in equities has not translated into demand for crypto,” it commented.

Macro asset weekly performance through Nov. 24. Source: Talos

Data from onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant also showed an imbalance between Bitcoin’s declines and recovery attempts. Over the past 30 days, downside volatility in Binance derivatives markets continued to exceed upside volatility.

Related: Bitcoin ETF November outflows top $5B, Morgan Stanley bucks trend

“That’s roughly 2.4 times more volatility on the way down than on the way up,” a CryptoQuant community analyst noted.

If the status quo remains, the analyst concluded, it would imply that the market is repricing Bitcoin incrementally lower.

BTC rolling 30-day upside vs. downside volatility. Source: CryptoQuant

BTC/USD remains above the realized price of the extant supply, a key trend line which has functioned as support since the end of the 2022 bear market. The pair has nonetheless traded below it in every past bear market, with the longest phase totaling 301 days.

#4994. Europe’s only spot bitcoin ETF starts trading in Switzerland, BIT says

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

BIT Asset Management's BBIT fund debuted on SIX Swiss Exchange with 350 BTC in assets and a 0.19% annual expense ratio.

BIT Asset Management's spot bitcoin ETF has begun trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange, with the company saying it is the first ETF in Switzerland to hold bitcoin directly.

The fund trades under the ticker BBIT in U.S. dollars and Swiss francs. It debuted with 350 BTC (currently worth over $20 million) in assets and has a total expense ratio of 0.19% a year. BIT said BBIT is currently Europe's only spot bitcoin ETF.

The Jacobi FT Wilshire Bitcoin ETF was Europe's first spot bitcoin ETF when it debuted on Euronext Amsterdam in August 2023. Euronext has listed the fund as inactive since Feb. 2, 2026. Jacobi Asset Management (Holdings) Ltd appointed a liquidator on Feb. 26, 2026, as part of a creditors' voluntary liquidation, according to a notice in The Gazette.

BBIT is publicly offered only in Switzerland. BIT pointed to investors outside the U.S., including Asian investors who hold assets with Swiss private banks, as a potential audience. It did not specify which investors outside Switzerland could buy the fund.

"If investors want a US product, they have plenty of choice. If they want a non-US product in a neutral jurisdiction, until now they really didn't," said Cynthia Wu, co-founder and chief commercial officer of BIT. "BBIT gives investors outside the US a regulated, liquid way to hold Bitcoin through the bank or broker they already use, with the asset protection of a fund."

The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, or FINMA, approved BBIT on Oct. 20 after an 18-month review, according to BIT Asset Management. FINMA exempted the fund from diversification rules, allowing it to invest entirely in bitcoin.

Most bitcoin products listed in Europe are structured as debt securities, BIT Asset Management said, noting that BBIT is a Swiss investment fund. The firm said Swiss-regulated AMINA Bank holds the fund's bitcoin assets separately from BIT Asset Management's own assets. BBIT also allows in-kind subscriptions, letting investors exchange bitcoin directly for ETF shares without first converting it to cash.

"The economic exposure of a fund and a note can look very similar when everything goes well. The difference is what happens when it doesn't," said Friedrich Herzog, chief investment officer of BIT Asset Management. "The segregation of duties and responsibilities of counterparties is by design, and it is why products like this take years to build and approve."

BIT Asset Management was previously known as Crypto Finance (Asset Management) AG. BIT said the group acquired the Swiss asset manager in 2024 and renamed it Matrixport Asset Management AG before it took its current name.

The BBIT listing comes as bitcoin has fallen back below $60,000. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw about $4.94 billion in net outflows in November through Tuesday, according to SoSoValue data. The U.S. ETFs began trading in January 2024.

#4993. Ukraine Passes Law to Legalize and Tax Its Crypto Market From July 2027

Ukraine Passes Law to Legalize and Tax Its Crypto Market From July 2027

Ukraine's parliament has passed a law to legalize the country's crypto market and tax virtual asset transactions, with the new rules set to take effect on July 1, 2027.

The Verkhovna Rada approved bill No. 10225-d in its second reading and as a whole on Wednesday, with 271 lawmakers voting in favor, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, first deputy chair of the parliament's finance, tax and customs committee, said on Telegram. The law still needs to be signed by President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Zhelezniak said the law would bring in an extra 15 billion hryvnias (around $330 million) in budget revenue.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Under the law, individuals will pay 18% personal income tax and a 5% military levy on profits from crypto transactions, according to state news agency Ukrinform. Swapping one crypto asset for another will not be taxed, and losses from previous years can be carried forward.

For crypto bought before the law takes effect, a reduced rate will apply when holders cash out into traditional currency during 2027 and 2028: 5% plus the military levy. Zhelezniak wrote that the reduced rate would apply to "the entire volume," rather than only to profits.

Oversight will be split between the National Securities and Stock Market Commission and the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU). The central bank will be responsible for stablecoins, and can set its own rules for their use, including allowing or banning their circulation.

The NBU will also authorize and supervise issuers of e-money tokens and providers that exchange virtual assets for traditional money, the central bank said in a statement, according to Interfax-Ukraine.

Ukraine first moved to legalize crypto in 2021, and Zelensky signed a law on virtual assets in March 2022, weeks after Russia's full-scale invasion. Soon after, the NBU banned purchases of crypto with hryvnias.

The new bill, which adds tax rules and aligns Ukraine's regulation more closely with the EU's as part of its bid for membership, passed its first reading in September 2025.

Ukraine has also explored other ways to bring crypto into the state's orbit. Lawmakers submitted a bill to create a strategic crypto reserve in June 2025, and in June 2026, the country placed more than $8.3 million in seized USDT under state management for the first time.

#4983. The 11 Best War Movies About Brotherhood, Ranked

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Ahead of Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl, we’ve pulled together a list of gripping films that show how bonds between men survive—and sometimes break—under fire.

DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football. The director of Friday Night Lights has returned to a world of cocksure young players with their whole lives ahead of them in dire need of rousing their morale—only now it’s the true story of the football game between two World War II Marine regiments at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. There’s another connection: both The Mosquito Bowl and Friday Night Lights are adapted from books by author Buzz Bissinger.

Berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service. After enduring years of the Pacific campaign, they realize how valuable the team spirit and camaraderie of football can be as the Battle of Okinawa looms ahead of them.

The Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood. The deeply felt connection between soldiers is the lifeblood of historical war films; when done convincingly, a squad’s well-earned devotion and loyalty add rich melodrama to the action. Brotherhood is just as compelling when it is subverted—like the respect felt between soldiers on opposing sides, or when hardened, broken combatants struggle to express the empathy and compassion they feel. The best war movies know that brotherhood endures after the fighting stops, but in different forms—softer, stranger, when it’s hard to reconcile the memories of war with a world that continues as normal.

To mark the Thanksgiving release of The Mosquito Bowl on Netflix, we ranked the most gripping and rousing war films about brotherhood.

An ensemble of actors you'd typically see in a "Young Stars of Tomorrow" profile immerse themselves in a U.S. Navy SEAL platoon and recreate a real-time Iraq War firefight that co-director Ray Mendoza was a part of. Opening with the platoon jubilantly dancing to "Call On Me" streamed through their base's crappy internet, Warfare quickly adopts a stripped-back and meticulous play-by-play of how one slice of warfare was actually experienced. You get a sense of brotherhood from the practiced, reflexive interactions between SEALs, and their interdependence also helped build the film, as Mendoza and co-director Alex Garland drew from the testimonies of his fellow soldiers when writing the script. The stylistic choices—like a thundering sound mix and infrequent use of satellite photography—add an extra layer of tension to Warfare's depiction of courage under fire. It’s one of the most visceral movies in recent memory about modern war.

Before he brought us high-octane visions of robot cops and ambitious showgirls, Paul Verhoeven directed a handful of smash hits in his native Netherlands, including this Golden Globe-nominated war epic about the diverging fates of Dutch students during the Nazi occupation. Led by a supremely dashing Rutger Hauer, Soldier of Orange begins in 1938 and follows the wartime trajectory of Erik Lanshof, an initially neutral but increasingly principled aristocrat who protects his Dutch Resistance friends and distances himself from fascist collaborators. Before long, his entire school group has pledged one type of loyalty or another. Observed over a period of time, war reveals everything, and Erik’s blossoming heroism emerges as a result of his friendships all changing—for better or worse.

Forgive us for taking a creative approach to the headline so early in the list: Hell in the Pacific features no battles or squadron camaraderie, and takes place on a deserted island with only two characters—an American pilot (Lee Marvin) and a Japanese army captain (Toshiro Mifune)—who don’t understand a word the other person says. Even without comprehension, the American and Japanese soldiers find a hundred ways to rile each other up, including shock tactics, sabotage, pranks, and even makeshift imprisonment. Gradually, they realize each other’s company is the strongest connection to their starving humanity available to them, even if they’re affected in a way they can’t explain. Free from the rhetoric and politics of war, Marvin and Mifune play men who slip into a state of brash, stubborn childishness, and a brotherly kinship forms in spite of their inherent opposition.

Clint Eastwood and Steven Spielberg sound like an odd pair to collaborate on a war picture, but Eastwood’s pared-down, melancholic visual style is a terrific fit for this post-Band of Brothers war movie. Flags of Our Fathers wasn’t received as positively as its Japanese-language companion film Letters from Iwo Jima, but it’s a robust and affecting watch—splitting its runtime between the overwhelming Battle of Iwo Jima and its aftermath, where three soldiers celebrated as the iconic “flag-raisers” spent the final year of the Pacific Campaign on a spiritually draining propaganda tour. Flags of Our Fathers takes the essential themes of war cinema—brotherhood, sacrifice, heroism—and juxtaposes them with the United States military manufacturing their own national images and narratives in real time. The tension between the brutal experience of being a brother-in-arms and the sanitized version promoted by war’s survivors makes for a powerful watch.

It’s as if director David Ayer (Suicide Squad, Bright) made a WWII movie to hammer home two points: tank warfare was a nightmare, and soldier hazing was way more hardcore than what you see in Band of Brothers. In the final months of the war in Europe, Wardaddy (Brad Pitt) rolls his bloody and battered tank unit slowly toward Berlin, and the arrival of fresh-faced pencil-pusher Norman (Logan Lerman) gives the hardened squad a chance to berate and bully the newcomer about all the ways he is soft, and war is hell. As their fellow brothers-in-arms are increasingly blasted apart into viscera, Wardaddy’s take-no-shit squad bolsters their unsentimental unity, and each of the five traumatized brothers rely on each other to watch their back and keep them sane on a frontline that might as well be the border to hell.

Spike Lee’s bracing film about the scars of Vietnam takes a familiar concept—a jaded band of veterans who try to pull off a heist—and spins it in a thorny, unpredictable direction. Four older Black veterans (led by an intense, captivating, and Oscar-snubbed Delroy Lindo) return to ‘Nam to recover the CIA gold their squadron hid during the war—aside from a delayed payday, it’s also the ultimate memorial of their late squad leader Norman (Chadwick Boseman). Marked by years of bitterness and PTSD, the “Bloods” retrace their steps while juggling painful reflections on how the war left them angry and guilty. When they're ambushed in the jungle and have to pick up guns again, we're reminded that Lee is never satisfied sticking in one narrative mode for too long, but the jagged catharsis of cranky, once-loyal soldiers confronting their wounds is far more visceral to watch.

When Private Alex (Harry Styles) says, “We're regimental brothers, mate,” in the belly of a fishing trawler on Dunkirk Beach, he’s not acting nobly—he’s making the case for throwing a soldier he thinks is German (he’s actually French) to the Nazis surrounding them. So much of Christopher Nolan’s war film about the perilous evacuation of Allied troops from France’s northernmost beaches centers on division: soldier feuds, breakdowns in communication, and a nonlinear narrative that takes place over a week or an hour depending on who’s in front of the camera. But Dunkirk’s staggering disaster and survival action builds to an overwhelming climactic sense of unity. Across every mini-arc and timeline, Nolan shows us countless pairs of soldiers, pilots, and civilians who stand together as symbolic brothers.

After the famously gnarly and disorienting D-Day beach landing sequence—which has influenced every WWII action movie since, including The Mosquito Bowl—Saving Private Ryan settles into the most iconic band of brothers story outside of… well, Band of Brothers, co-created by this film’s director and star. Tom Hanks is the grouchy uncle leading a reluctant squad to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (Matt Damon) from the front lines after his brothers were killed in action. The squadron's trudge through France is fueled with banter, grumbling, and the type of resentment that stews between siblings who hate when someone receives special treatment. Steven Spielberg’s gift for balancing movie-star gravitas and off-the-cuff charisma is on full display in the ensemble, but no gruff, hot-tempered soldier has a response to Private Ryan's justification for not returning to his mom: “Tell her that when you found me, I was here, and I was with the only brothers I have left.”

The only war film on this list to be set before the 20th century and at sea, the Napoleonic Wars-era Master and Commander has a reputation for being a “dudes/gentlemen rock” classic: the reputation still holds up. Under the command of Captain Jack Aubrey (Russell Crowe), the HMS Surprise wages war against a French frigate that taunts the crew across the seas. Majestic naval battles aside, much of Master and Commander has a warm hangout tone, focusing on the kinship between Aubrey and ship’s surgeon Maturin, their interest in classical music and botanical science, and revelrous suppers in the captain’s quarters. It's impossible to watch Peter Weir’s sea epic and not pine for the brotherly loyalty (maybe not the seasickness or cannonball attacks) that Aubrey inspires here. Nothing will make you feel the romantic thrill of adventure like Master and Commander.

Pick your favorite scene from The Deer Hunter: the riotous wedding party, the spontaneous Frankie Valli singalong over a game of pool, or the exacting game of Russian roulette played by prisoners of war. They each shine a light on the ordinary, working-class brotherhood that was completely transformed by the Vietnam War. This Oscar-winning epic builds complex, traumatized characters (played by Robert De Niro, John Cazale, and Christopher Walken) who reckon with never being able to experience their relationships and community in the same way again. The Deer Hunter paints such a disturbing and fragile picture of the “before and after” of Vietnam, as each brotherly bond becomes charged with alienation and despair. Notorious for its multiple “death game” sequences, The Deer Hunter excels in making its harrowing portrayal of war and PTSD genuinely heartbreaking.

One of the best things to come out of legendary Hong Kong filmmakers John Woo and Tsui Hark falling out was the future director of Hard Boiled and Face/Off leaving the iconic A Better Tomorrow series to make this searing war story. Beginning in the late ’60s, it focuses on three close friends (Tony Leung, Jacky Cheung, Waise Lee) whose smuggling ambitions dunk them headfirst in the brutality and desperation of the Vietnam War. Bullet in the Head blends the epic sweep of New Hollywood war epics (Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter) with Woo’s “heroic bloodshed” toolkit, which meant electric action spectacle and bold, tragic melodrama. An underrated operatic beast in Woo’s stacked filmography—not to mention a personal one, as Woo used the film to express his reaction to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre—the action is always in service of a high-stakes tri-friendship that can only take so much passion and betrayal before the treasured brotherhood breaks.

Rory Doherty is a critic and journalist based in Edinburgh, Scotland. His work can be found at British GQ, Vulture, Inverse, AV Club, and other publications. He can be found on Twitter/X at @roryhasopinions

#4981. ‘The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens’: Zcash team urges faster deprecation of legacy shielded pool

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

About 400,000 ZEC remains in the Sapling pool, worth about $291 million at current prices.

Zcash Zcash (ZEC) infrastructure team Zakura urged the network to accelerate the deprecation of its legacy Sapling shielded pool, citing speculation of mathematical breakthroughs at AI labs.

In a post early Thursday, Zakura recommended users migrate any ZEC still in Sapling to Ironwood. These shielded pools allow users to hold and transfer ZEC without publicly revealing transaction amounts or sender and recipient addresses.

"The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens," the team wrote.

While practical breaking of the pairing-based cryptography used by Sapling remains highly speculative, Zakura also recommended a network upgrade to disable payments into Sapling. Roughly 400,000 ZEC, or approximately 2% of supply, remains in the pool, according to Zakura, worth roughly $291 million at current prices. Zakura said most wallets support both Sapling and Ironwood, and the impact should be minimal, with miners accounting for much of the activity left in Sapling.

"Less than 2.6% of all transactions in the last 30 days use Sapling, and of those, 66% are known miner flows, and it's highly likely most of the remainder are miners as well," the team said.

An earlier Zcash forum proposal in April had suggested waiting a year after a community decision to make Sapling withdrawal-only. At the time, the proposal put its balance at 600,000 ZEC, down from 1.1 million at the start of 2024. Zakura did not suggest a new deadline in its Thursday post.

Zakura pointed to a reported proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and unsubstantiated rumors that AI labs had also made advances in integer factorization, the process of splitting large numbers into their prime factors. The difficulty of that task underpins RSA encryption, which is rarely used in cryptocurrencies, according to the team. Zakura said some math can be used for attacks on both RSA and pairing-based cryptography, so advances in one could help with the other, but the reported Riemann proof and the rumors do not show that either can be broken in practice.

"Practical pairing breaks are highly speculative," Zakura said, adding that transparent transactions and Ironwood do not rely on factoring or pairings.

Nevertheless, a hypothetical break in Sapling's pairing-based proof system would allow forged proofs, Zakura said, putting the funds in the pool at risk. The same cryptography does not secure users' private keys or their cryptographic records of shielded funds, so the team said developers could replace the proof system without replacing those records. However, Zcash would have to freeze Sapling before an attack compromises its state and users could then later recover their funds using a new ECDLP-based or hash-based SNARK, Zakura said.

Separately, the Ethereum Foundation doubled its protocol security team, The Block previously reported, arguing that AI is a "more urgent risk" than quantum computing and recommending Keccak-256 over four competing candidates for Ethereum's planned shift to hash-based cryptography. Zakura said it is also working on a proposal to add hash-based, post-quantum signatures for Zcash transparent transactions using SPHINCS+ with 192-bit security.

#4980. Vitalik Buterin calls for verifiable chips as hardware wallet threats evolve

Buterin warned that future attacks could use lookalike chips with hidden malicious functions, making hardware tampering harder to detect.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin on Thursday called for enhanced verifiability in computer chips, citing evolving security threats in the hardware wallet sector.

Buterin said in a blog post that most commercial open-source chips do not disclose enough detail to verify their physical construction. Publishing what a chip is programmed to do is different from providing a blueprint against which inspectors can check the hardware itself.

“This concern is not just theoretical,” Buterin said, adding that the crypto industry has seen attacks that involve inserting spy implants into hardware wallets before they get sold to consumers.

Buterin warned that future attacks could be harder to detect, with malicious functions built into replacement chips that resemble legitimate ones.

“This, you cannot detect with the naked eye,” he wrote.

In October, Ledger said malicious implants in devices sold through reseller CryptoBilis captured recovery phrases and transmitted them over cellular networks. Ledger suspended reseller sales in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, tightened distribution rules and offered X-ray inspections after tampered devices surfaced beyond the region.

Trezor in November said it found similar implants in three devices sold through the same reseller. The company released a firmware update to stop the implants from capturing data and reduced its reseller network by about 80%.

Related: Ledger’s early implant warnings deserved more action, Karpelès says

Buterin warned that inspecting chips would remain a specialist task for professional auditors, journalists and civil society groups, even if hardware designs became fully open-source.

“In order for computation to be democratized, the hardware layer must be open for participation and tinkering too,” he wrote.

Still, Buterin said that given extreme commercial pressures that companies face, the industry cannot expect all hardware to become open source.

He said he hoped the industry would split into performance hardware and secure hardware. While secure hardware might be “10x less efficient or more,” it would still be sufficient for most everyday applications.

Elon Musk’s X has won a default judgment in a UK court against two men accused of running a network of Bitcoin-focused accounts that gamed the platform’s creator-payout system, a case that prompted Musk to warn fraudsters: “Don’t mess with X.”

London’s High Court entered the judgment on Nov. 20 against Vivek Kumar Sen and Zamyang Sherpa after neither man filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, with Master Teverson ruling in favor of X without a trial.

A default judgment means the court entered the order because the defendants failed to engage, not because the allegations were tested and proven. Either defendant can apply within seven days of being served to have the order varied or set aside.

The case dates to a claim issued Sept. 21, when X sued the pair and unidentified accomplices for allegedly operating a coordinated bot army to inflate engagement and siphon money from its Creator Revenue Sharing program.

Crucially, the judgment awards no money yet. Because X sued for “an unspecified sum,” the order states the amount of damages and interest will be decided later at a separate Disposal Hearing.

X has estimated the improperly obtained revenue at no less than £207,384 (about $271,000) and said it is seeking at least £75,000 ($98,000) more in investigation and remediation costs. Those are the company’s claimed figures, not sums the court has granted.

X General Counsel James Burnham announced the ruling, writing that the company had “sued people who abused Creator Revenue Sharing by operating a network of accounts to manipulate engagement” and that the court had now entered judgment against two of them.

“We aren’t kidding around,” he added. “Fraudsters worldwide: Do not mess with X.” Musk reposted the statement with his own terse endorsement.

Even once damages are set, recovering the money is a separate matter that depends on whatever assets Sen and Sherpa hold.

The case reflects the broader strain of the “engagement economy,” where platforms paying creators based on activity have become targets for coordinated manipulation.

X retired Creator Revenue Sharing, which launched in 2023 and paid out based on engagement, on Sept. 7, replacing it the next day with Original Content Rewards, a system it says emphasizes original material over raw engagement volume, a shift partly aimed at the kind of gaming alleged here.

#4976. JPMorgan says bitcoin ‘capitulation’ signaled by Strategy’s record-low NAV multiple

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

JPMorgan said Strategy's NAV multiple has fallen to around 0.88x, below the previous low seen in late June.

JPMorgan analysts said the recent drop in Strategy's valuation relative to its bitcoin holdings to a record low signals "capitulation" in the bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) market.

The ratio has fallen to around 0.88x, below the previous low seen in late June, JPMorgan analysts led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a Wednesday report. The analysts' charts compare Strategy's enterprise value with the dollar value of its bitcoin holdings, though the report does not specify the exact formula used.

Strategy has its own way of calculating the ratio, which it calls mNAV. The company divides its common share price by the dollar value of its net bitcoin holdings per share, taking into account its debt, preferred claims, and U.S. dollar assets, according to its website.

Strategy's dashboard showed an mNAV of 0.88x at 10:39 a.m. ET on Nov. 25, which later rose to 0.94x. Both figures are based on Strategy's own calculation.

"The premium to NAV collapses to a new record low of 0.88 for MicroStrategy’s stock, signaling capitulation in bitcoin," the analysts wrote.

Bitcoin has fallen back to around $60,000 after recovering briefly from last week's lows.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), the largest spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund by market capitalization, continued to see outflows even during the brief price recovery, the analysts said. "Indeed, the speed of the outflows has, if anything, been more intense than the outflows from early May to late June this year," they added.

Last week, the analysts said retail investors likely drove much of the recent crypto ETF outflows and may have sold to buy stock ETFs. They also said bitcoin's price drop had widened the gap between its market price and their estimated production cost of around $86,000, likely adding pressure on higher-cost miners to sell bitcoin from their reserves.
