#4916. New York Wins $1.37B Judgment Against NovaTech Founders Who Fled the US

New York Wins $1.37B Judgment Against NovaTech Founders Who Fled the US

A New York court has ordered the founders of collapsed crypto trading platform NovaTech to pay $1.37 billion for running a Ponzi scheme that targeted Haitian immigrant communities, Attorney General Letitia James said on Wednesday.

Cynthia and Eddy Petion, along with NovaTech and related companies, are jointly liable for $1.13 billion in disgorgement plus $232.5 million in interest, for a total of $1,367,023,585, according to court documents in the case, which is before Justice Anar Rathod Patel in the Commercial Division of New York's Supreme Court.

We won a historic $1.3 billion judgment against the founders of crypto company NovaTech for defrauding hundreds of thousands of people, including Haitian immigrants in New York.

We'll always fight to bring fraudsters who take advantage of New Yorkers to justice.

— NY AG James (@NewYorkStateAG) November 25, 2026

Cynthia Petion and AWS Mining, a crypto mining company the couple promoted before founding NovaTech, were also ordered to pay a further $6.2 million combined for the AWS Mining scheme.

"NovaTech cruelly targeted immigrant families through faith and community groups with the promise of a better life while robbing them of their life savings," James said in a statement.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The judgment follows a default ruling in August 2025, after the Petions fled the country and failed to respond to the lawsuit. That ruling also banned them from the securities, commodities and crypto industries, and the court then decided how much they owed.

In October, James' office asked the court to set the damages at about $1.37 billion. The Petions failed to comply with a court order to provide a full accounting of payments to and from investors, according to the court documents.

Collecting the money may prove difficult. The couple was allegedly living in Panama when James first sued in June 2024, Reuters reported at the time.

James' office sued NovaTech and AWS Mining in June 2024, alleging that they targeted immigrant communities, particularly Haitian New Yorkers, through prayer groups, social media and WhatsApp chats, with false promises of high returns, while running illegal pyramid schemes. The schemes defrauded hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide, including about 11,000 New Yorkers, according to the attorney general.

The Securities and Exchange Commission charged the Petions and NovaTech promoters in August 2024, alleging the firm raised more than $650 million from over 200,000 investors.

Four promoters in the New York case, Martin Zizi, Frantz Ciceron, Ricardo Roy Sr. and James Corbett, have agreed to pay nearly $6 million and have been permanently banned from the securities, commodities and crypto industries.

#4913. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.

#4911. Japan weighs tighter oversight of DeFi, self-custodial wallets

Japan’s financial regulator is exploring measures to curb illicit finance risks, including potential restrictions on access to DeFi services.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency (FSA) is weighing potential new regulations for decentralized finance (DeFi) and self-custodial wallet providers as part of a broader effort to address risks associated with onchain finance.

In a discussion paper dated Thursday, the regulator raised the possibility of discouraging users from accessing DeFi services that lack adequate Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing controls.

The FSA also asked whether regulated businesses that interact with DeFi, including stablecoin issuers, on- and off-ramp providers and financial institutions, should play a role in mitigating illicit finance risks when no party responsible for regulatory compliance can be identified.

The regulator questioned how to identify parties responsible for DeFi services that claim to be decentralized but retain centralized elements, and whether front-end providers that give users access to decentralized exchanges should be subject to financial regulation.

The question of who should be held responsible for DeFi activities remains unresolved in other major markets. The European Union excludes fully decentralized crypto services without intermediaries from its Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation, while US regulators have largely focused on the nature of financial activities and the degree of control exercised by developers or operators. The stalled US CLARITY Act seeks to clarify which DeFi participants should be subject to financial regulation.

The FSA noted that direct regulation of self-custodial wallet use and providers that solely develop or sell software or hardware remains uncommon internationally but raised questions about whether additional measures are needed to protect users and prevent illicit financial activity.

Japan already requires domestic virtual asset service providers to collect information and maintain records on transactions involving self-custodial wallets, according to the FSA. Potential anti-fraud measures also include cooling-off periods for transfers from newly opened crypto exchange accounts to self-custodial wallets.

The discussions form part of a broader financial strategy announced by the FSA in July to promote onchain finance, with the initiative’s interim findings targeted for early 2027.

#4909. UK Regulator Cites Binance Hack as It Plans Tougher DeFi Rules Than US and EU: Report

UK Regulator Cites Binance Hack as It Plans Tougher DeFi Rules Than US and EU: Report

Britain's Financial Conduct Authority plans to require decentralized finance platforms to be authorized under its incoming crypto rules, taking a harder line than regulators in the U.S. or EU, the Financial Times reported on Thursday.

FCA officials told the newspaper they were deliberately strict on DeFi because they saw a high risk of fraud, scams and money laundering, and because users had little ability to recover stolen funds or seek compensation.

The regulator pointed to the record $6.4 billion hack of Binance in October. While Binance is a centralized exchange, the hackers moved large sums through decentralized exchanges, which do not freeze stolen funds, swapping them into other tokens to make them harder to trace.

"The speed and scale at which stolen funds move through DeFi platforms can frustrate attempts to freeze and block" transfers, Jane Moore, the FCA's head of department for payments and digital assets, told the FT.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The FCA's position means UK-regulated crypto trading platforms will not be allowed to execute retail trades on DeFi platforms. Moore said that divide between the regulated and unregulated sectors was deliberate, given the lack of consumer protections in DeFi.

The regulator also plans to require all UK retail orders for equities, tokenized or not, to be executed on a regulated platform, cutting off access to offshore DeFi venues for tokenized stocks. The same risk should be treated the same way, Jamie Bell, the FCA's head of capital markets, told the newspaper. The FCA and the Bank of England have set out a shared vision for tokenization within the regulated system.

After consulting on its wider crypto rules earlier this year, the FCA in October published draft guidance on how its rules apply to firms providing services that use or interact with DeFi. The consultation closed on November 18, and the regulator expects to publish final guidance in January 2027, ahead of its crypto regime taking effect on October 25, 2027.

Crypto firms argue the approach will leave UK investors without access to products such as tokenized equities and decentralized lending.

Linda Jeng, chief legal and policy officer at Aave Labs, which builds products for decentralized lending protocol Aave, called the FCA's position "highly problematic" and has written to the regulator asking it to clarify which DeFi service providers its rules would cover, according to the FT.

Coinbase's head of policy in Europe, Katie Harries, said that where the U.S. and EU are building rules for regulated DeFi access, the UK is "creating a prohibition." In September, the EU's European Securities and Markets Authority proposed a new regulated service under the bloc's MiCA rules for crypto firms that give customers access to DeFi protocols.

UK trade group CryptoUK has also urged the FCA not to treat DeFi developers as regulated by default, warning in its consultation response that parts of the proposed guidance go further than the law.

Orest Gavryliak, chief legal officer at DeFi aggregator 1inch, argued that financial crime is a challenge across all of finance, and that DeFi's transparency is a strength. "Every transaction is recorded on a public ledger, so illicit flows can be traced in a way that closed systems do not allow," he said.

A one-size-fits-all approach "would limit access to innovation without meaningfully reducing risk," Gavryliak said, adding that regulators could draw on industry tools such as wallet screening to design proportionate, risk-based rules.

Harry Halpin, CEO of decentralized VPN provider Nym, told Decrypt that a truly decentralized DeFi platform would be very hard to regulate, since there should be no central party to oversee. "If the government attempts then to block or censor access to these platforms, and so slowly built a Great Firewall of Britain, people will simply use a VPN," he said.

#4908. Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

Why women are turning to the EDM scene in the name of mental health.

Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try new experiences.

That’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with new friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she says. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

Manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

“There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

The EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

The older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady says. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”

Samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she says. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”

For some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter new eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist at Madison Liddle Therapy and co-founder of The Practice Co, a co-working space for therapists. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

Hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”

Getting out and meeting new people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she says, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own company—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

In fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” says O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

The physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially important with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle says.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, says co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

Raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

Alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” says Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

Of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study said they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

However, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley says. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”

Karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

But Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she says. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”

Wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” says Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

Manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier shows with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”

However, Manson prefers later shows because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she says. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.)

Despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she says. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”

But she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she says.

Rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” says O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she says. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

Midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”

Since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try new things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she says, “so seize the moment.”

#4904. Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

Here’s what experts say about the “promising” new study results.

While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer. Specifically, once they hit your stomach, nitrates and nitrites found in these foods can spark a chain reaction called nitrosation that allows carcinogens to develop. This isn’t just a meat-eating issue either: fruits and vegetables that have grown in areas affected by pollution can also lead to this chain reaction.

Now, new research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement. It can cut this chain reaction and, in theory, lower the odds that carcinogens will develop after eating certain foods linked to this reaction, according to the findings.

Researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon. But the findings raise a lot of questions about why this may work and how to actually put it into practice in a safe way. Here’s what the researcher behind the study and dietitians want you to keep in mind.

Meet the experts: Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo; Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; and Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

For the study, researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body, and where they undergo chemical changes. The model looked at a range of areas, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma (i.e. the liquid part of your blood). Researchers discovered that having vitamin C alongside foods that contain nitrates and nitrites may halt chain reactions that happen in the body, including nitrosation, which makes substances that are linked to cancer development.

The researchers also looked at whether taking vitamin C after each meal could help, and found that it may reduce the formation of nitrosation products linked with cancer risk. The boost was most meaningful when people had foods that contained nitrates and nitrites, like salami, bacon, and other processed meats.

The researchers also theorized that this may explain why certain types of produce that happen to contain both vitamin C and nitrates (like spinach) don’t seem to increase cancer risk, while others do.

It’s important to stress this: The study was based on a mathematical model and was not a clinical trial or data analysis. Because of that, it's hard to draw too many conclusions right now.

Still, this link isn’t out of nowhere. “Under acidic conditions in the stomach, nitrites can undergo chemical reactions that lead to the formation of potentially harmful N-nitroso compounds,” says Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo. “Vitamin C can interfere with these reactions, reducing the formation of these compounds.”

Why vitamin C? “Vitamin C is an antioxidant,” points out Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Meaning, it helps to neutralize unstable molecules in the body—and may do the same for nitrosation.

But the effectiveness of vitamin C depends on when it’s in the stomach compared to when these reactions happen, McNicol adds. “Our simulations suggest that taking vitamin C shortly after meals could be particularly effective, as this allows vitamin C to overlap more closely with periods when nitrosation would otherwise be relatively high,” he says.

Experts stress that it’s important to keep the study in perspective. “While the findings are promising, more research is needed to determine whether taking vitamin C after meals actually reduces cancer risk,” says Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

Cording agrees, stressing that while the findings are “promising,” they’re still just based on a mathematical model at this point. “That said, getting enough vitamin C and other antioxidants, alongside nutrients like fiber and other beneficial plant compounds, has been associated with reduced risk of disease and with overall immune system function,” Cording says. “There are lots of great reasons to include vitamin-C rich fruits and vegetables throughout the day.”

There are other things to consider, like practicality and safety. “Our research does not establish that taking vitamin C supplements after every meal is necessary or advisable,” McNicol says. “Although our simulations suggest that dividing a fixed daily supplement across meals may be more effective than taking the same amount at once, further experimental and clinical studies are needed to determine whether these strategies are effective and safe in people.”

High doses of vitamin C from supplements can also lead to GI discomfort, including nausea and diarrhea, Gans points out.

For now, this is more of an interesting finding vs. an actual dietary recommendation. “Until we have more research, there's no reason to recommend intentionally adding extra vitamin C, whether from food or supplements, after every meal specifically to reduce cancer risk,” Gans says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#4903. Galaxy Research Withdraws Call That Bitcoin's Bear Market Is Over

Galaxy Research Withdraws Call That Bitcoin's Bear Market Is Over

Galaxy Research has withdrawn its call that Bitcoin's bear market ended in June, saying the signal that underpinned it has failed.

"We withdraw our call that the bear market ended in June," the firm wrote in a report sent to clients on Tuesday. It said a daily close below Bitcoin's June 30 closing low of $58,525 would mark "the start of a move to a materially lower low."

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Bitcoin is currently changing hands at around $60,600, up 3.4% over the past 24 hours, according to Decrypt data. It fell as low as $57,308 during that period, as inflation data and proposed U.S. tariffs weighed on markets.

In an October 26 report, Galaxy's head of research, Alex Thorn, argued that Bitcoin had bottomed in June, in part because it had climbed back above its 50-week moving average in September after 44 weeks below it. In past cycles, such a sustained recovery above that average had only come after a bear market's low.

That reclaim lasted seven weeks. Bitcoin closed below the 50-week average in the week ended November 8, and the following week fell below its 200-week average, which Galaxy describes as historically the floor. The October report had set a tripwire: a weekly close back below the 50-week average that was not regained within a month. To regain it by around December 8, Bitcoin would need to rise almost 22% from its November 22 close. "We are not waiting for it," Galaxy wrote.

On an intraday basis, Bitcoin has already set a new bear market low, falling to $55,100 on November 21, below its July 1 intraday low. On closing prices, the June 30 low of $58,525 is still intact.

In seven previous bear markets in which Bitcoin closed below a low that had held for at least 60 days, the eventual bottom came at least 17% lower, with a median of 52%, according to Galaxy. Applied to the June low, that would put Bitcoin at about $48,500 at the shallowest and $28,200 at the median.

The firm said the evidence points two ways. By the calendar, this bear market is already older than any before it, 412 days after Bitcoin's October 2025 record. By depth, it looks unfinished: Bitcoin's 53% decline compares with 77% to 93% in previous bear markets, and it has not yet closed below its realized price of $53,205, the average price at which all coins last moved, something every prior bear did for at least 140 days. Only two of the 13 bottom signals Galaxy tracks have been met.

Galaxy said a weekly close back above the 200-week average, now $68,159, and then the 50-week average, now $74,401, would move it back toward its October view.

Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Decrypt he agreed the market remained in a bear phase, but said a longer bear market need not mean a deeper one. As Bitcoin is pulled into global asset allocation, its price is driven increasingly by "macro liquidity, interest-rate expectations, and institutional risk appetite, rather than solely following the crypto market's traditional four-year cycle," he said.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $453.1 million in net outflows on Wednesday, their seventh straight day of withdrawals, according to SoSoValue data. That brings November's net outflows to $5.39 billion, extending the funds' worst month on record.

Options traders are also positioning for further declines. Bitcoin's put/call open interest ratio on Deribit rose to 0.82 last week, its highest in more than a year, according to a weekly report from digital asset trading platform Talos.

"BTC's muted rebound shows the relief in equities has not translated into demand for crypto," Tanay Ved, senior research associate at Talos, said in the report. "Until short covering turns into net buy pressure and sustained spot demand, the move remains fragile heading into thin holiday liquidity."

#4901. UK is ‘getting it wrong’ on DeFi regulation, says Coinbase

Coinbase and Stand With Crypto argue that the FCA’s proposed DeFi rules could leave UK users without regulated access to decentralized finance.

Coinbase and Stand With Crypto, a crypto advocacy group backed by the exchange, are pushing back against the UK’s proposed approach to decentralized finance (DeFi), arguing that restrictions on regulated crypto platforms could leave consumers with fewer safeguards when accessing DeFi services.

The criticism follows reports on Nov. 26 that the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) plans to proceed with tighter rules and authorization requirements for DeFi platforms, citing money laundering risks exposed by the $6.3 billion Binance hack. Although the attack targeted a centralized exchange, hackers moved stolen funds through decentralized protocols, complicating efforts to trace and freeze the assets.

Katie Harries, head of policy for Europe at Coinbase, said the proposals could limit opportunities for regulated firms to work with authorities on consumer safeguards.

“The UK is getting its approach to DeFi wrong,” Harries told Cointelegraph. “This isn’t a ban on UK consumers using DeFi; it’s a ban on giving them a regulated route to use it.”

In an October opinion piece for Cointelegraph, Harries argued that the proposed framework could effectively prevent regulated crypto platforms from offering DeFi services, as requirements to execute customer orders through authorized trading venues could exclude decentralized protocols with no central operator capable of obtaining FCA authorization.

Related: Japan weighs tighter oversight of DeFi, self-custodial wallets

Harries argued that regulated platforms could help address the FCA’s concerns around DeFi through due diligence and safeguards.

The FCA has previously used regulatory sandboxes to allow financial services firms to test new products in live markets under regulatory oversight. On Feb. 25, the regulator named four regulated entities to test out stablecoin products within its regulatory sandbox.

“The UK has got a lot right on crypto, but its approach is closing the door on DeFi innovation,” Harries said.

Harry Pearce-Gould, general manager at Stand With Crypto, argued that the proposals could leave UK users with fewer options for accessing DeFi services. “That leaves UK crypto users without the trusted, regulated routes to access DeFi that will be available to people doing the same thing in other jurisdictions.”

He said people should be able to use crypto for financial activities such as borrowing against their holdings, provided they have clear information about the associated risks.

The implications could extend beyond consumer protection, potentially putting the UK at a competitive disadvantage in the digital asset industry, according to Harries. “The UK is creating a prohibition, and that doesn’t sit right with its ambition to be a global centre for digital assets,” she said.

The FCA closed consultations on its proposed DeFi guidance and wider crypto regulatory framework on Nov. 18, with final guidance expected in January 2027. The new regime is scheduled to take effect on Oct. 25, 2027.

#4900. 7 Golf Club Sets for Beginners That Will Have You Lowering Your Handicap

Sets from Callaway, Stix, and more offer solid, affordable clubs.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU’RE JUST getting into golf, there will be a time in your life when you need to invest in a golf club set. As it’s a lifetime pursuit, it’s best to invest in a decent setup, and if well maintained, it can last you for years to come. While advanced players may want to customize their own golf club sets, there are numerous brands that make complete sets that will have you playing from day one. Even notable brands like Callaway and Wilson have solid options.

It's true you could go buy pre-owned clubs as your first beginner set, which is not a bad idea to peruse your local Dick's Sporting Goods or local golf shop (especially for previous year model demos during the offseason), brand sites' used portals like Callaway Certified Pre-Owned, or eBay. But if you've gotten the golf bug and are looking for a new-to-you set, these days golf brands are churning out shiny, high-quality sets at affordable entry points. Customization is also better than ever, as several outfitters offer club length adjustments, different club combinations, and a selection of stylish golf bags to accompany them. You can always ask for a set as a great golf gift, too.

Whichever route you choose, we spoke with Paul Silva, head pro at NYC’s Van Cortlandt Golf Club to answer some of the most frequently asked questions when it comes to buying a beginner golf set. After you get a legit set, don't forget about some golf shoes.

When it comes to the game of golf, not many brands can boast expertise in every single category. One that can though is Callaway. The brand behind elite golf balls, top-tier putters, golf bags, pro-worthy irons and drivers, Callaway is no slouch when it comes to making high-quality gear for beginners.

The 2026 XR lineup comes in a 13-piece set, which includes a mallet putter made by Odyssey and its DFX V-line Fang shape, which offers higher stability and more aggressive alignment aids—two elements you’re rarely going to find in an entry-level putter. The irons are classics, based on decades of stellar game-improvement technology, while the hybrids, 3-wood, and driver are modeled after one of golf’s most exciting new weapons of the past couple of years, the Paradym. This year you also get an approach wedge. Add on the fact of its high-MOI V-Line putter and you get a set that dominates the short game. This set will set you back more than most, but don’t be surprised if you tote these clubs along with you for the next ten years.Read More: The Best Golf Shirts

Though technically a slightly older legacy bundle, this platinum set features two premium features we love. The first is the irons. They're well-built and just what you want out of a beginner iron, making them a solid set to build the base of your arsenal for years to come. Considered a game improvement set, they have a thinner top line and are more refined. The second is the golf bag: It's highly comfortable thanks to the dual carrying strap and lightweight design, and comes with ample pocket space.

Wilson is a brand with immense golf pedigree—no player worth their salt will scoff at the brand’s gear, whether you’re shooting even par or 20-over. The set is immensely affordable, so while it will probably long outlast your golf career, it won’t make you feel bad about upgrading once you start to improve.

For someone just getting into the game or hitting the range for the very first time, this set is great to start with. With every club you’ll need to get from the tee box to the green (and probably everywhere in between), this set won’t leave you without an option, no matter how wayward your shots get.

The set has a solid 4.3-out-of-5-star rating on Amazon, with reviewers lauding the set’s value and high level of forgiveness. Odds are high you’ll want to upgrade sooner than later, but if you or someone you know likes to pick up new hobbies, this set will help decide if golf is a lifelong commitment or just a phase.

While one of the most expensive of the bunch, this TaylorMade set is certifiably legit. We're talking about a beast of a driver which features an adjustable driver, allowing you to change the loft and face angle as your swing evolves (something you hardly ever find on a complete set driver), a beautiful set of high-performance irons, and a stylish golf bag that will protect your investment with reassurance.

This is a set for those who are getting serious and playing several times per week. The barrier to entry is higher than the rest of the options on our list, but when you consider the pedigree of a brand like TaylorMade, you’ll find that the long lifespan of the clubs and golf bag make it a set you can grow into and not have to replace for years.

Picking up on the game quicker than you thought? You can skip the early stages and go for a complete set that allows you to learn how to optimize your shot-making skills. The Stix Perform Set is a complete 12-club set that will provide you with all the tools you need, all for under $1,000.

The Perform Set is the brand’s first set with the option for irons with a steel shaft, a boon for mid-high handicap players whose higher swing speeds may be a bit too much for the extra flex of graphite. Clubs that benefit from the flex (the driver, 3 wood, and 4 hybrid) still come standard with graphite, but having the choice when selecting irons is going to greatly increase the amount of time you’ll stick with your Stix.

In my testing, I took the Stix out for a couple dozen rounds, walking and riding in a cart. The set is very manageable size-wise. The bag is light enough for comfortable wear but big enough to stay secure when strapped to the back of a golf cart. They’re some of the most forgiving clubs I've played and are well-built, resulting in improved distance and fewer mishits. My favorite club was the 4 iron hybrid—I've never hit a hybrid so well.

Another set from one of the most prestigious equipment brands in golf, the Cobra Fly XL set is the ideal set for someone who knows they’re going to be consistently hitting the golf course in a golf cart. The cart bag is big, sturdy, and spacious, while the wide range of clubs gives you options in every part of the course.

The Cobra brand is well-recognized, and these striking clubs will fit in with any other sets on the course, ensuring that your skills do the talking, not your equipment. If your skills are lacking, that’s okay, too, because each club in this set is super forgiving thanks to excellent weight distribution and optimized shape, from the driver right down through the putter.

When you’re looking for a little more performance but still trying to stay affordable, PXG is a brand to look to. This Wildcat Bundle is an extremely versatile setup that utilizes premium materials and the same tech found in the brand’s standalone clubs, all tuned for maximum forgiveness and easy launch—must-haves for beginners.

While it is a hefty investment, they’re the one-and-done purchase type, meaning that you won’t outgrow them anytime soon, and will last for years to come. These clubs are meant to bridge the gap from big box store generic clubs and a custom-fitted pro set, while providing a fairway-friendly driver and the brand’s polymer cores for a softer feel and more distance. While it’s only a 9-club set, it has all the essentials you’ll need to make it up and down on any course.

Most beginner sets will include between nine and 11 clubs. 10 is a good sweet spot; it is enough to have a driver, a fairway wood and/or a hybrid, a 5i-9i, a wedge, and a putter. Generally a full set is 14 clubs; that includes the putter—and you can keep no more than that number in your bag during play.

Two recommendations we would make would be to forego a 3-wood in favor of a 5-wood or 4-hybrid—most players don’t actually need a 3-wood and would be better served with a more forgiving hybrid (or two). If you can, consider adding a sand wedge (or potentially a lob wedge that you learn how to use) to sit alongside your pitching wedge, as many pitching wedges aren’t lofted enough for tricky shots in the sand or around the greens.

As Silva told us, "I tell everyone the same thing in the beginning, find a few clubs that you can hit—a hybrid, a 5 iron, a 7 iron, a pitching wedge, a putter. You can learn to do a lot with those things, especially in the beginning. You don’t need to worry so much about distance."

Most beginners will want a shaft made of graphite. These will create greater swing speeds, allowing you to hit the ball further, even as you start to tune your swing. If you’re not a full-on beginner or aren’t looking for any extra distance, a set with steel shafts are a great choice. These will be easier to grow into skill-wise, making it easier to adapt as your game improves. As your swing speed improves, the flex of graphite shafts will be too much, and you’ll need to graduate to iron shafts then.

The main factors in forgiveness are club head and shaft. There’s a lot to dig into with this (we could write an entire essay on these two things), but in general, most beginner sets are outfitted with the absolute easiest club head to hit and a graphite shaft that allows for greater swing speed and fewer mistakes. We’d say not to get caught up in the nitty-gritty and focus on finding a set that is made for new players—something that almost every brand will outline in its product descriptions. Make sure you take a look to see what handicap each club set is designed for and pick the one made for high handicappers (that’s you), as these are coined as player improvement clubs.

Golf club prices run the gamut, but a good set of beginner clubs will usually run you anywhere from $250 to $1,000. This is a huge discrepancy, but there is a big range in quality from bottom to top. If you’re a brand-new golfer, spending $1,000 isn’t necessary, but if you think you’re in it for the long haul and want a set of sticks that are going to allow you to progress without having to upgrade, spending a little more cash is a great idea—the technology really does make a difference and it'll save you with an upgrade in a year or two if you improve.

To help facilitate the best golf club sets on the market in 2026, I consulted with Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower (a mid-handicapper himself) to determine which clubs available are truly worthwhile. We evaluated each on club head size, materials, shaft construction, and forgiveness. Some sets, like the Stix full setup, gave us the chance to see what a quality set of clubs can do for a high handicapper, while the more affordable sets gave us a good idea of what is possible at a low price point. Even for someone like me, who may only get on the links a couple of times a year, using any of the sets listed below can have an instant improvement in gameplay. Brower typically plays around 20 rounds per year, so he definitely knows his way around a course. Ultimately, we picked sets that we liked the most, but there are so many options today, you really can’t go wrong when you’re trying to make a decision, because, hey, you can always upgrade.

Beginners to golf do not need to get a custom fitting for clubs, but if you have the money and want to go all in on your new hobby, then we won't stop you. Really the main measurement you want to get right when buying is proper club sizing (not too tall or too short)—and the good news is most of these clubs will have a solid fit for just starting out.

The only initial adjustments you need to make as a beginner are if you are exceptionally tall or short. If you are over 6'2" consider sizing a half-inch or more length adjustment on your clubs. You can also just opt for a set that has a "Tall" option available. If you are under 5'5", you'll likely want a half-inch decrease in length adjustment.

If you like to go by feel, swinging your friends’ clubs or talking to a pro at your local course will help confirm the sizing you need. As you progress in your game, sizing can be pinpointed down further to personalized club sizing, if you choose.

There's nothing wrong with buying pre-owned clubs to serve as your first beginner set. There is a whole market online for really nice pre-owned clubs for a solid price on sites like Ebay and the golf brands' websites. Yet the downside is, you guessed it, they were somebody else's. There's wear and tear on them.

Instead of buying pre-owned, opt for new. A new set will give you the proper tools to get acclimated on the course and really give you the opportunity to learn the game. Golf is a lot about feel. Your clubs should be your best friend out on the course, not some raggedy set whose best days are long gone.

Buying a new set also gives you something to build off of. As you get better you'll want to make upgrades. Maybe you want a more precise sand wedge or a driver with more power? What you'll do next is swap out single clubs one at a time until you find a set that fits your game to a T.

#4899. Jade Cargill Was a Basketball Player Before the WWE. Here’s What Changed Everything

The 34-year-old wrestling superstar stops byThe Huddle ahead of her appearance on Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28th.

Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade says that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

“I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”

Despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she says.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

Jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

“I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”

Jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she says. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

“I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she says. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

“I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade says. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”

As a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she says. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”

And when a new opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she says. “And look at me now.”

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#4897. Standard Chartered's Zodia Custody Says Hackers Accessed Client Contact Details

Standard Chartered's Zodia Custody Says Hackers Accessed Client Contact Details

Zodia Custody, the crypto custodian owned by Standard Chartered, has confirmed that an unauthorized party accessed some client and employee information in a security incident this week.

The firm detected attempts to probe its platform on November 23, and temporarily took its business-to-business (B2B) API offline while it put additional security measures in place before restoring the service, CEO Richard Clark said in a statement posted to X on Thursday.

We are aware of media reports regarding a recent security incident. Richard Clark, CEO of Zodia Custody:

"On 23 November, we detected attempts to probe our platform. As a precaution, we temporarily took our B2B API offline and implemented additional security measures before…

— Zodia (@ZodiaCustody) November 26, 2026

The following day, Zodia's monitoring found that an unauthorized party had accessed "limited client information," Clark said. That consisted of publicly available details about client organizations and, for a small number of clients and employees, a business contact name and email address.

"Based on our investigation to date, there have been no unauthorised transactions," Clark said. Zodia has contacted its clients and informed the relevant regulators.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Reuters first reported the breach on Thursday.

An API, or application programming interface, lets institutional clients' systems connect directly to Zodia's platform. Zodia did not say who was behind the incident or how the information was accessed.

Exposed names and email addresses can be used in targeted phishing attacks, in which criminals impersonate a trusted firm to trick victims into handing over credentials or funds.

The incident comes weeks after Standard Chartered signed definitive agreements on October 21 to acquire 100% of Zodia Custody. Once the deal completes, subject to regulatory approvals, Zodia's custody business will be folded into the bank's existing digital asset custody operations, while its software business will move to a new SC Ventures entity, Zodia Solutions.

Standard Chartered's venture arm first moved into institutional crypto services in 2021. Since then, the bank has been expanding its crypto offering. In July, it became the first global bank to get direct access to Circle's USDC stablecoin, and last month it launched Bitcoin and Ethereum trading for clients.

#4895. Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

The six-week postpartum checkup was never meant to be about fitness.

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that new moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.)

The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually says, and how to approach working out in this new chapter of life.

In many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport says. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”

These traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an important medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

The first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering says. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

To come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.)

Based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here

Pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport says. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport says. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport says. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

At the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” says Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”

For some new moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”

In fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye says. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!)

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, says Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you quickly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

There can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

And if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

Amy is a freelance writer and editor who covers health, fitness, and lifestyle topics—with a focus on practical advice that fits into real life. She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. Her work has been published in Women’s Health, Men’s Health, SELF, Wondermind, HGTV, Outside, REAL SIMPLE, The New York Times for Kids, and more. Amy lives in central New York where she spends her off-hours chasing after her two kids, digging into backyard gardening projects with her husband, and creatively squeezing at-home workouts into her schedule as often as she can.
